column3: Doors at Ögedeibulag are shut at dusk, and the edge of town is left empty after dark.
This is how Ögedeibulag looks on a first visit; a season there might show it differently.
Ögedeibulag has no line and no force, and the threat now at hand has noticed both.
The hamlet settles things itself, quickly, and does not always settle them well.
Ögedeibulag's pay book is always behind: its defenders are paid late or not at all, and people owed wages are slow to turn out when trouble comes.
You can walk into Ögedeibulag from any direction and pass nobody on the way in.
If Ögedeibulag were attacked, its people would fight with no leaders and no plan, each household for itself.
Ögedeibulag sends whoever it can against things they are not trained for, and pays for it each time.
Ögedeibulag's defense is conventional throughout. What arrives unseen here goes undetected and therefore unanswered.
Ögedeibulag could deal with a brawl or a thief, but the hamlet could not hold off a raid.
The beasts give Ögedeibulag no rest between attacks, and each one costs the hamlet something it cannot quickly replace.
Ögedeibulag should come through this crisis if nothing else goes wrong, though its defence has had to change to meet it.
Ögedeibulag is too small to wall, and what has come for it now makes the smallness a danger rather than a protection.
Ögedeibulag's books record no gang, guild or racket: what wrongdoing the hamlet has, people do on their own account.
No criminal's money appears in the Elder Council's accounts at Ögedeibulag, so what the hall spends is spent on the hamlet.
